title: The Hot Archive

scenario.situation: Storage costs have ballooned: seven years of raw logs are sitting on hot storage, and the bill is climbing 20% quarter-over-quarter.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The engineering team believes the root problem is the vendor's pricing and wants to open discount negotiations with the cloud provider.
scenario.question: Is the vendor's price the real driver — or is something else inflating the bill?

decisions.prompt: The team is ready to call the vendor. How do you frame your investigation before anyone picks up the phone?

options.label: Benchmark vendor pricing against competitors
options.detail: Pull quotes from AWS, GCP, and Azure to see if the current per-GB rate is above market.
options.consequence: You find the vendor is roughly at market rate. The negotiation team has no leverage, and the underlying cost driver hasn't been examined at all.
options.divergenceCost: Anchored on the team's hypothesis and skipped diagnosing the actual data estate.

options.label: Diagnostic access audit — segment data by last-query recency
options.detail: Query storage metadata and access logs to categorize every dataset by when it was last read, before assuming the problem is price.
options.consequence: You surface a clear recency distribution across the estate. The shape of that distribution tells you immediately whether the issue is price-per-unit or what is sitting on which tier.

options.label: Project cost growth forward and set a budget alert
options.detail: Model the 20% QoQ trend and alert leadership when a threshold is crossed.
options.consequence: You have a well-formatted forecast, but costs keep rising — you've measured the symptom without diagnosing the cause.
options.divergenceCost: Optimized monitoring of the problem instead of investigating its source.

options.label: Immediately design a data deletion policy to free space
options.detail: Propose purging logs older than two years to cut volume.
options.consequence: Compliance raises an objection: several log cohorts are under a seven-year retention mandate. You've proposed a solution that creates legal risk before understanding the data.
options.divergenceCost: Jumped to a solution before knowing retention obligations or actual query patterns.

decisions.prompt: Access logs are in hand. Which metric do you use to characterize what is actually driving the hot-storage bill?

artifact.title: Raw storage volume by data age bucket (TB)
artifact.caption: Raw TB on hot storage per age bucket. The oldest buckets are largest — but volume alone doesn't tell you whether that data is being read.

options.label: TB stored per age bucket
options.detail: Use raw storage volume by data age as the primary signal.
options.consequence: The oldest buckets are largest, which looks alarming — but you don't know if anyone is querying that data. High volume on hot storage is only a problem if the access pattern doesn't justify the tier.
options.divergenceCost: Read storage size as the signal without normalizing for whether the data is actually hot.

options.label: Query-access rate by age bucket (% of stored objects queried in last 90 days)
options.detail: For each age bucket, compute what fraction of stored objects received at least one read in the past 90 days.
options.consequence: The normalized view is unambiguous: access rate collapses to near zero past the 90-day mark, yet those buckets account for the overwhelming majority of hot-storage spend. The discount conversation becomes irrelevant.

artifact.title: % of objects queried in last 90 days, by data age bucket
artifact.caption: Access rate by age bucket. Data older than 90 days is almost entirely unread yet lives on hot storage — the real cost driver, not the per-GB rate.

decisions.prompt: Access rates crater past 90 days, and those cold buckets account for ~85% of the hot-storage bill. What do you tell the team?

options.label: "Vendor pricing is irrelevant — implement lifecycle policies to cold/archive immediately."
options.detail: Make the causal call and recommend acting now.
options.consequence: You're directionally right, but the mandate ignores two open questions: whether any low-frequency workloads have latency requirements that rule out archive tiers, and whether aggregating old logs is safer than raw tiering. Without that check, a rushed rollout could break a quarterly compliance report that no one flagged.
options.divergenceCost: Overclaimed certainty and skipped validating edge-case access patterns before recommending action.

options.label: "Price isn't the lever — 95%+ of data past 90 days is unread on hot storage. Lifecycle tiering likely cuts cost far more than a discount. Let's validate low-frequency workload SLAs and run a staged pilot before full rollout."
options.detail: Present the finding, name the remaining uncertainty, and propose a safe path to action.
options.consequence: The team shelves the vendor call. The pilot confirms one quarterly compliance job needs a slightly warmer tier for two days at month-end — a small carve-out — and the rest tiers cleanly to cold/archive, cutting the bill by over 60%.

insight: The cost explosion had nothing to do with the vendor's rate card: ~95% of stored data was never touched after 90 days yet sat on the most expensive tier for years. The team's instinct to negotiate was a plausible but wrong lever — the real driver was tier misclassification, not price-per-unit. The core lesson is that storage cost is a product of both volume and tier appropriateness; access-recency segmentation, not raw volume or vendor benchmarking, is the right diagnostic. Cutting costs here means matching data temperature to tier, not haggling over the bill.
